1261.title: The bhog
1261.hook: the close of a complete reading, with the last pages, Anand and Ardas
1261.howItsDone: At a bhog, family and sangat gather for the final pages of the Guru Granth Sahib; Anand Sahib is sung, the Ardas is said standing, a hukam is taken and karah prashad is shared, often followed by a meal in the langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sehaj path: the whole Granth in order, at a walking pace, named for poise. Your line was your own pace.

The room has been quiet for days, one reader's voice after another. Now it's filling up. Cousins arrive from across town. Somebody's grandmother is helped to a spot near the front. Children are hushed and sat down. The reader is close to the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and everyone has come to hear the last pages together. A whole reading, whether it was unbroken or slow, is about to close. How it closes has a name, and a shape, and the shape carries its own teaching.
screen: `THE ROOM FILLS UP.` → `THE LAST PAGES, TOGETHER.` → `HOW IT CLOSES HAS A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: The word is bhog. In Sikh use, it names the close of a complete reading of the Granth. First come the last pages. Near the very end is a short passage called the Mundavani, the seal, by Guru Arjan. In paraphrase: in this platter three things have been placed, truth, contentment and contemplation, and with them the Name, the support of all; whoever eats of it, whoever enjoys it, is saved. So the Granth ends by describing itself as a meal. Everything read over those days turns out to have been a plate set before the sangat. Communities differ on where the reading stops, at the Mundavani or carrying on through the Ragmala that follows it, and the code notes that difference and leaves it to custom. Then Anand Sahib is sung, Guru Amar Das's song of bliss. Anand means bliss, and the reading closes not with a sigh of relief but with joy. Then everyone stands for the Ardas, the prayer that remembers the Gurus and asks for the Guru's grace, and the reading is offered up. A hukam is taken, and karah prashad, the sweet offering, is shared, which is tomorrow's story. Look at what the bhog refuses to do. It doesn't let the last page just run out, the way a phone call can drop. It gathers people. It names what was received. It gives thanks out loud. It asks forgiveness for any mistake in the reading. Then it feeds everyone. A long reading ends not by stopping but by being completed.
screen: `BHOG: THE CLOSE OF A READING.` · `THE MUNDAVANI'S PLATTER.` · `ANAND SAHIB, THE SONG OF BLISS.` · `THE ARDAS, THEN A SHARED OFFERING.` · then, large: `END WELL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that ended well, a goodbye at an airport, a last day at a job, a hard conversation that closed with a hug, and notice what made it good: who was there, what was said out loud. Then think of something in your own life that's ending soon, and what it would take to end it well.
Bhog. The close of a complete reading: the last pages, Anand Sahib and the Ardas, and then a shared offering. Today's word.
Your line: end well. A plate set before everyone, and thanks said out loud. Until tomorrow.

1262.title: Making karah prashad
1262.hook: equal parts flour, sugar and butter, cooked while reciting
1262.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, karah prashad is prepared from equal parts flour, sugar and ghee while Gurbani is recited, presented with Ardas, and handed to everyone in the congregation in cupped hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhog: the last pages of a full reading, the Anand and the Ardas. Your line was end well.

Flour, sugar, butter. Three ingredients on a counter, and nothing about them looks holy. Then the flour goes into a heavy pan with the melted butter, and someone starts to stir. It darkens slowly, pale to gold to the color of an old coin, and the kitchen fills with a warm, toasted smell. Sugar dissolved in water goes in with a hiss. And all the while, the cook is saying something under their breath. Not a shopping list. Words of the Guru. At the end of a gurdwara service, this is what lands in people's hands.
screen: `FLOUR, SUGAR, BUTTER.` → `STIRRED UNTIL GOLDEN.` → `WORDS UNDER THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Karah is the deep iron pan, and prashad is a gift given by grace: grace from the pan. The Sikh Rehat Maryada gives the recipe, in paraphrase: equal parts wheat flour, sugar and clarified butter, prepared in a clean vessel by someone who has bathed, reciting Gurbani while it cooks. Start with the measure. Equal parts: no ingredient is the star, and nothing a plain kitchen doesn't already have. Next, the cook. The code doesn't ask for a priest. It asks for clean hands, a clean pot and a mind on the Guru's words. The prayer isn't added at the end like a garnish; it's stirred in the whole time. Then the bowl comes into the congregation. The code describes stanzas of the Anand being recited and Ardas offered, and the prashad touched with a kirpan before it's shared. Last, the sharing. The code says it's given to everyone in the sangat alike, without asking about caste. Whoever you are, you hold out your hands, and the same sweet, warm handful lands in yours as in everyone else's. Some families make it at home too, with the same recipe and the same rule. A kitchen becomes a place of remembrance, and an ordinary chore holds the Guru's words for as long as the pan is on the fire.

segments.voice: Picture a small thing you'll cook soon, a pot of rice or a cup of tea, and choose the words you'd keep under your breath while you make it: a line of Gurbani, or simply Waheguru, if you pray; the names of the people who'll eat it, if not. Then sit with your hands open in your lap, the way people hold them out for prashad, and walk through it once in your mind: the pan, the stirring, the words.
Making karah prashad. Equal parts flour, sugar and clarified butter, made with clean hands while reciting Gurbani, then shared with everyone alike. Today's word.
Your line: pray while cooking. The prayer goes in with the flour, not after it. See you tomorrow.

1263.title: Katha, the explanation
1263.hook: exposition of Gurbani by a teacher
1263.howItsDone: In gurdwaras a katha may follow the kirtan: a teacher reads a passage of Gurbani and explains its words, setting and meaning to the congregation, while the Guru Granth Sahib remains open above.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karah prashad, stirred while the Guru's words were said. Your line was pray while cooking.

The kirtan stops. The musicians set down their instruments, and one person sits up at the front, near the Granth, without a harmonium. They read a single line of Gurbani aloud, slowly. Then again. Then they start to talk. Who wrote this line, and what was happening around it. What this one word means, and why the Guru may have picked it over another. A story from the Gurus' lives. Another line from elsewhere in the Granth that answers this one like an echo. A long while can pass on one sentence. Children who were fidgeting go still. This is katha.
screen: `THE MUSIC STOPS.` → `ONE LINE, READ TWICE.` → `THEN SOMEONE OPENS IT UP.`

segments.voice: Katha means telling, or a discourse. In the gurdwara it's exposition: a teacher taking a passage of Gurbani and explaining it to the sangat. Kirtan sings the word; katha unfolds it. The Sikh Rehat Maryada speaks to it directly. In paraphrase: in the congregation, only a Sikh may give katha, and the explanation must be in keeping with Gurmat, the Guru's teaching. That's a guardrail. Katha is an aid to the word, not a stage for the speaker's own opinions dressed up as scripture. Picture the shape of it. The Granth stays open, above everyone. The teacher sits lower, facing the people, holding a line up to the light and turning it. A good explanation doesn't replace the line; it sends you back to it, and now you hear more in it. Why it matters: Gurbani is poetry, written in old Punjabi and other languages of its time, packed with images of rivers, merchants, brides and fields. Without someone to unpack them, a listener can sing a hymn for years and miss what it's saying. Katha passes the meaning from one person who has studied to a room full of people who want to understand. Some teachers speak at length on a single word; others give a short talk before the evening prayer. Either way, words that were heard are now explained.
screen: `KATHA: TELLING, EXPOSITION.` · `ONLY A SIKH, KEEPING TO GURMAT.` · `THE LINE STAYS ABOVE THE TALK.` · `POETRY THAT NEEDS UNPACKING.` · then, large: `EXPLAINED.`

segments.voice: Take one word you've met on this path, like Waheguru, and say it once, slowly. Then ask it the katha questions, one at a time: what does each part mean, what picture is in it, where else have you heard something like it? Don't hurry to an answer; let the word sit above your thoughts and notice what opens.
Katha. Telling, discourse: the exposition of Gurbani by a teacher to the sangat, kept in line with the Guru's teaching. Today's word.
Your line: explained. A good explanation always sends you back to the line. Rest well.

1264.title: No caste, no charms
1264.hook: the code rejects caste, untouchability, charms, idols and lucky days
1264.howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks Sikhs not to believe in caste, untouchability, charms, omens, auspicious days, horoscopes or idol worship, so Sikhs who keep the code don't choose dates for weddings and other ceremonies by the stars.

segments.voice: Yesterday, katha: one line of Gurbani held up to the light and turned. Your line was explained.

A charm hung by the door to keep bad luck out. A wedding moved to another month because the stars were wrong. A family that won't let a certain neighbor drink from their cups. Scenes like these turn up in many times and places, the Gurus' Punjab among them. People reach for them because life is uncertain and a charm feels like control, or because a ranking of people feels like order. The Sikh code takes them up, one after another, and sets them down.
screen: `A CHARM BY THE DOOR, A STAR CHART.` → `A CUP NOT SHARED.` → `THE CODE SETS THEM DOWN.`

segments.voice: Back in year three, this path looked at caste and how the Gurus rejected it. Today, the code's own list. In its section on a Sikh's personal life, the Rehat Maryada names what a Sikh should not believe in. In paraphrase: caste, untouchability, magic charms and spells, omens, auspicious days and times, horoscopes, and the worship of idols. Two very different things sit together there. Caste and untouchability are about people: who counts as higher, who counts as unclean. Charms, omens and lucky days are about fear: trying to steer life with a thread or a calendar. In Sikh teaching, both put something else where God should be. Caste first. Guru Nanak, in a hymn in Raag Asa on Ang three hundred forty-nine, says in paraphrase: recognize the light in everyone, and don't ask about caste, because in the world beyond there is no caste. If the same light is in every person, a ladder of birth is a fiction, and a cup that can't be shared is a lie about the person holding it. That's why the langar is eaten side by side in rows, and why the prashad we met two days ago goes to everyone alike. Then the charms. In Sikh teaching, what happens comes within God's hukam, the divine order. A thread on the wrist can't bend it; a lucky Tuesday can't buy it. So a Sikh keeping the code doesn't wait for a lucky date to marry, travel or start a business; the day that works is the day. Every person carries the same light, and every day belongs to the same Giver.
screen: `THE CODE'S LIST OF REFUSALS.` · `CASTE: A LADDER OF BIRTH.` · `ONE LIGHT IN EVERYONE.` · `EVERY DAY WITHIN THE HUKAM.` · then, large: `NO LUCKY DAYS.`

segments.voice: Look gently at your own small habits, a lucky shirt, knocking on wood, a number you avoid, and pick one, asking what it might be guarding against. Then, just for this sit, set it down, and let the day ahead be a day, no luckier or unluckier than any other.
No caste. The Sikh code rejects caste and untouchability, and with them charms, omens, idols and lucky days, because the same light is in everyone. Today's word.
Your line: no lucky days. The day that works is the day, whatever the calendar says. Until tomorrow.

1265.title: Daswandh in the code
1265.hook: giving a tenth of earnings for the Guru's cause
1265.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep daswandh set aside a tenth of their earnings for the Guru's cause, giving to gurdwaras, the langar, education and relief, and some give part of it as time and service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the code's refusals: no caste, no charms, one light in everyone. Your line was no lucky days.

Payday. The money lands, and before it does anything else, it gets sorted. Rent here. Groceries there. Something for the phone bill, something for the car. Every household has its own version, on paper, in an app or in someone's head. Now add one more pile at the front of the line, set aside before rent, not after the fun. Not a tip from whatever's left over, but a share taken first and given away. Sikhs have a plain name for that share.
screen: `PAYDAY, SORTED INTO PILES.` → `ONE MORE PILE, AT THE FRONT.` → `A SHARE GIVEN FIRST.`

segments.voice: Daswandh means a tenth part. In Sikh teaching, it's a tenth of one's earnings, given for the Guru's cause, and it belongs to the way of life the code sets out for a Sikh. Three things to notice. First, what it comes out of: earnings, honest work. Sikh teaching joins remembering the Name, earning honestly, and sharing what you have, and daswandh sits where earning and sharing meet. Guru Nanak puts it in one line, on Ang twelve hundred forty-five, in paraphrase: the one who eats what they earn by their own work and gives some of it away from their own hand, that one recognizes the path. From your own hand, not someone else's pocket. Second, where it goes. The Guru's cause is wide. It can fund the langar, where anyone can sit and eat, keep gurdwaras open, support schools, and pay for relief when disaster strikes. Some Sikhs give it in money, others give part of it in time, serving in the kitchen or teaching children. Communities differ on how strictly to count. Third, the measure. A tenth is concrete: small enough to live with, large enough to notice. Giving whatever is left over depends on mood. A tenth, set aside first, turns sharing from a feeling into a habit, and the habit into a quiet partnership with everyone the langar feeds.
screen: `DASWANDH: A TENTH PART.` · `FROM HONEST EARNINGS.` · `FOR THE GURU'S CAUSE.` · `A MEASURE THAT MAKES A HABIT.` · then, large: `A TENTH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind what came to you lately, money, time or skill, and without doing any math, picture a share of it set apart first, before the other piles. Then let one place it could go come to mind, a food bank, a neighbor, a gurdwara kitchen, an hour for someone stretched thin, and if you pray, offer it quietly with the word Waheguru.
Daswandh in the code. A tenth part of honest earnings, given for the Guru's cause, set aside first. Today's word.
Your line: a tenth. Small enough to live with, large enough to notice. See you tomorrow.

1266.title: The turban in the code
1266.hook: the code asks men to wear a turban; women may choose to
1266.howItsDone: Sikh men tie a dastar to cover their uncut hair, often freshly each morning; Sikh women may wear one too or cover their hair with a chunni, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada leaves the turban optional for women.

segments.voice: Yesterday, daswandh: a tenth of honest earnings, set aside first. Your line was a tenth.

Early morning, in front of a mirror. A long strip of cloth, starched or soft, is shaken out and folded lengthwise. One end goes between the teeth to hold it. Then the wrapping starts: around, up, across, pleat by pleat, each layer laid flat over the last, the hands moving the way hands move after years of the same thing. A pin tucked here. A last pass at the front, checked in the mirror, nudged a finger's width. Done. It took a few minutes, and the whole day will be lived inside it.
screen: `A STRIP OF CLOTH, A MIRROR.` → `PLEAT BY PLEAT.` → `A WHOLE DAY INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Way back on day three, you met the turban as a crown you tie yourself. Today, the code. Dastar is the Sikh turban. The Sikh Rehat Maryada says, in paraphrase, that a Sikh man must wear a turban, and that for a Sikh woman it's optional. Some Sikh women tie a dastar every day; others cover their hair with a long scarf, a chunni. Both are within the code. Why a turban at all? It starts with the hair. Keeping the hair uncut, kesh, is part of the Sikh way, and the code asks Sikhs to keep it. A turban covers it, keeps it clean and tidy, and keeps the comb, the kangha, tucked inside. So the dastar isn't decoration on top of the faith; it's how the uncut hair, kept as a gift, is cared for. Then what it says. Sikhs speak of the dastar as a crown, given by the Guru. Tradition says that in the Gurus' world a turban could mark rank and nobility. On a Sikh head it's worn by a farmer, a teacher and a surgeon alike; nobody's turban is a lower one. And a crown carries weight. A Sikh in a turban can't blend into a crowd; a stranger may remember what they do as what a Sikh did. Some Sikhs call that the turban's quiet job: a daily reminder to act like someone the Guru crowned. That's why, for Sikhs who wear it, being told to remove it is no small thing. It isn't a hat. It's part of the self, tied fresh each morning.
screen: `THE CODE: MEN WEAR IT; WOMEN MAY.` · `IT COVERS AND KEEPS THE KESH.` · `A CROWN FOR EVERY HEAD.` · `A CROWN CARRIES A WEIGHT.` · then, large: `CROWNED.`

1267.title: Naming a child
1267.hook: a hukam is taken and the child named with the first letter of the hymn
1267.howItsDone: Sikh families bring a new baby to the gurdwara with karah prashad; a hukam is taken from the Guru Granth Sahib, its first letter is announced, a name beginning with it is chosen, and Singh or Kaur is added.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dastar: the turban over the uncut hair, which Sikhs call a crown. Your line was crowned.

A new baby asleep in a car seat on the carpet of a gurdwara. Grandparents on one side, a nervous father on the other, the mother holding a bowl of karah prashad. Hymns of thanks are sung. Then the person attending the Granth opens it, not at a marked page but wherever it falls, and reads the hymn at the top of the left-hand page. Everyone leans in for one thing: the first letter. Somebody whispers a name they've been hoping for, and it fits. Somebody else is already counting names on their fingers. That letter is where this child's name begins.
screen: `A BABY IN A CAR SEAT.` → `THE GRANTH OPENED WHERE IT FALLS.` → `EVERYONE WAITS FOR ONE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Naam karan means the naming. The Sikh Rehat Maryada describes it, in paraphrase: when mother and child are able, the family comes to the gurdwara with karah prashad. Hymns of joy and thanks are sung. A hukam is taken, the way we met last week: the Granth opened at random and the hymn at the top of the left-hand page read. The first letter of that hymn is announced, and a name beginning with it is chosen. Then the code adds a second name: Singh for a boy, Kaur for a girl. Ardas is said, and the prashad shared. Two things to hold. First, who chooses. The Granth gives a letter, not a name. People still choose, so the name is both gift and choice: the Guru's word and human love meeting on one letter. Second, the second name. The code gives a boy Singh and a girl Kaur, whatever family they're born into. Some readers see a quiet answer to caste in that: a surname can carry a caste, and Singh and Kaur carry none. Earlier this week the code said no caste; here, some would say, it's written into the name. And the week, looking back: end well, pray while cooking, explained, no lucky days, a tenth, crowned, and now the name from the hukam, where a life's name begins in the Word.
screen: `NAAM KARAN: THE NAMING.` · `A HUKAM GIVES THE FIRST LETTER.` · `A NAME CHOSEN FROM THE LETTER.` · `SINGH OR KAUR FOR EVERY CHILD.` · then, large: `THE NAME FROM THE HUKAM.`

segments.voice: Say your own name once, slowly, in your head, and think about who chose it and what they might have hoped. If you know its meaning, hold that for a few breaths; if not, hold the hope instead, then let the name rest the way a hymn rests after it's read.
Naam karan. The Sikh naming: a hukam is taken, the first letter of the hymn is announced, a name is chosen from it, and Singh or Kaur is added. Today's word.
Your line: the name from the hukam. A letter from the Guru, a name from the people who love you. That's a week, done.
